title: Relative constructions and unbounded dependencies
description: Explore wh, that and bare relatives, integrated and supplementary clauses, fused relatives, and the long-distance gaps that connect them.
example: The report that the committee finally published confirmed what everyone had suspected.

key_terms.definition: A cover term for relative clauses and fused relatives, including NP and PP types.
A clause containing an overt or covert element interpreted through an antecedent.

The element in a relative clause that is linked anaphorically to the antecedent.

A relative clause containing a relative word such as who, which or whose.

A non-wh relative with no relative word or that.
A relative clause integrated into the nominal it modifies, prototypically restricting its denotation.
A prosodically detached relative clause adding information about an antecedent.
The relative clause following the foregrounded element in an it-cleft.
A relative construction in which antecedent and relative clause are fused into one phrase.
The initial phrase in a wh relative, containing the relative word and any material that percolates with it.
A word such as who, whom, whose, which, where or when used in a relative construction.
The spread of a relative feature from a word to the larger phrase containing it.
A relative phrase containing more than the relative word itself, such as whose house or with which.
A relative use that delimits the set denoted by the head nominal.
A relative use that adds information without restricting the antecedent’s denotation.
A detached element related to an anchor without being a syntactic dependent.
A relative clause with an infinitival verb, such as a place to watch the procession from.
A non-finite clause with an understood non-subject element supplied by context.
A fused relative phrase headed by what, whoever or whichever and functioning as an NP.
A fused relative phrase based on where or when and functioning as a PP.
An interrogative clause asking for a value, contrasting with a fused relative.
A relation in which a gap can be embedded arbitrarily deeply inside the clause.
A gap that is licensed by another gap in the same construction.
A construction in which an elided VP is interpreted through an antecedent containing the elided material.

intro: *The things that your father was saying* and *what your father was saying* pick out the same set of remarks. One is a noun phrase with a clause attached; the other is a single phrase in which the antecedent and the clause have fused. The pair is a good place to begin, because the difference between them is the difference between a relative clause and a relative construction.

Relative constructions come in several shapes. A relative word can carry the link, a subordinator can accompany a gap, or the gap can stand alone. The clause can be integrated into a nominal, detached as a supplement, or built into a cleft.

Behind all the variety is one question: how does the missing or anaphoric element get interpreted? A wh relative links a relative word to an antecedent and leaves a gap to mark the original function. A bare relative leaves only the gap. A fused relative folds antecedent and relativised element into one phrase. The rest of the chapter works through the consequences.

blocks.text: *I agree with most of the things that your father was saying* contains a relative clause modifying *things*. Replace the noun phrase and the clause with *what your father was saying* and the meaning survives, but the grammar changes: *what* now does the work of both the antecedent and the relativised element. That is a fused relative.

The traditional term *relative clause* is too narrow for the whole family. *What your father was saying* is a noun phrase, not a clause, and the corresponding forms based on *where* and *when* are prepositional phrases. *Relative construction* is the cover term that lets the clause and phrase types sit together.

The syntactic difference matters. A relative clause can be separated from its antecedent, which is what makes *the things [that your father was saying]* analyzable as two pieces. A fused relative cannot be split that way, because *what* is holding both pieces at once. That is why the fused type needs its own analysis rather than a footnote under relatives.

sections.title: Formal types: wh, that, and bare relatives

blocks.text: Take *the toys you don’t want*. Nothing in the clause marks it as relative: no wh-word, no *that*, just a gap where *toys* would be understood. Add *that* and the clause has a subordinator; add *which* and it has a relative pronoun. English offers three formal routes to the same relation, and they are not interchangeable in every position.

*Which* in *the toys which you don’t want* is a pronoun linked to *toys*. Replace it with *that* and the word is no longer a pronoun: it is the subordinator familiar from content clauses, and the object position is a gap. Remove both and the gap has no company at all.
Position constrains the choice. A subject relative in the non-wh form needs *that*; an object relative tolerates all three forms, which is why *the advice my neighbour gave me* sounds unremarkable.

sections.title: Integrated, supplementary, cleft, and fused relatives

blocks.text: Begin with two sentences that look alike but behave differently. *The boys who defaced the statue were expelled* uses its clause to narrow the set of boys; *My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida* uses its clause to add a fact about a man already identified. The first is integrated, the second supplementary. Two further relational types complete the set: the cleft relative, which follows the foregrounded element in an *it*-cleft, and the fused relative, which combines antecedent and clause in a single phrase.

Integration is primarily a matter of information structure. The boys who defaced the statue are a subset of the boys, and the clause is what tells you which subset. A supplementary relative does not narrow anything: *my father* already picks out one person, and *who retired last year* adds a fact about him. The clause adds; it does not select.

Cleft relatives belong to the cleft construction rather than to the nominal system, and their internal structure differs in ways that are easy to overlook. Fused relatives are further removed again: they are phrases, not clauses, and their antecedent is not a separate word at all but part of the same phrase.

blocks.text: In *the letter that drew our attention*, nothing sits in the subject position after *that*. The clause has a hole, and the antecedent *letter* supplies what belongs there. That hole is the gap, and the element it stands for is the relativised element. In a wh relative a relative word makes that element visible; in a non-wh relative the gap does all the pointing. Either way the gap keeps the grammatical function the element would have had: subject, object, complement of a preposition, adjunct or predicative.

In *I accepted the advice which my neighbour gave me*, *which* sits at the front and the gap sits after *gave*, where the object belongs. The pronoun is interpreted as object because the gap is an object. Put the gap in subject position, as in *the letter that drew our attention*, and the clause has no overt subject at all.

The gap is what separates a relative clause from a content clause. *The suggestion that Kim made* has one; *the suggestion that Kim cheated* does not. The words *that Kim* appear in both, which is why the gap has to be diagnosed rather than heard.

blocks.text: In *the people whose house we are renting*, the relative word does not arrive alone: it brings *house* with it. A wh relative begins with a phrase, and that phrase may be a single word such as *which* or a longer one such as *whose house* or *the result of which*. The extra material travels with the relative word to the front of the clause, even though only the word itself is linked to the antecedent.

The relative feature percolates upward from the word to the phrase that contains it. *Whose* lends its relative status to the noun phrase *whose house*; *which* lends it to the prepositional phrase *with which*. The whole phrase is fronted, but the antecedent relation runs through the word, not through the phrase as a whole.

The patterns are systematic rather than arbitrary: a prepositional complement can pass the feature to a PP, a PP complement of a noun can pass it to an NP, and genitive *whose* or determinative *which* can pass it to a larger NP. Infinitival and gerund-participial clauses provide two more routes. The table sets out all seven; percolation, not fronting alone, explains why such long phrases can open a relative clause.

blocks.text: Relativisation reaches most grammatical functions. Subjects relativise in *the letter that drew our attention* and objects in *the advice which my neighbour gave me*; genitive determiners relativise too, though the relative word has to change to *whose*. Complements of prepositions, adjuncts and predicatives are also available, with more constraints.

The dependency can cross clause boundaries. In *the man who she said had won*, the gap is the subject of *had won*, inside the content clause that *said* takes as complement. *Who* is linked to a position several clauses down, and nothing in the grammar sets a limit on how far down it can go.

Some functions are harder to reach than others. Adjunct relativisation usually wants a wh-phrase or a preposition, as in *the day when we met* or *the place where they stayed*. Manner and reason relatives are more restricted still. What licenses the gap depends on the relative word, the antecedent and the function the gap fills.

blocks.text: *The boys were expelled* says something about all the boys. Add *who defaced the statue* and the claim narrows to a subset. That narrowing is the characteristic work of an integrated relative: it sits inside the nominal, shares its prosody, and helps fix what the nominal refers to.

The clause usually sits right against its head: *the boys who defaced the statue*, not *the boys were expelled who defaced the statue*. That adjacency is part of how the antecedent is identified. The pattern has extensions: a relative can modify a superlative, as in *the fattest he has ever been*, or an interrogative pronoun, as in *Where can we eat that isn’t too expensive?* These are peripheral, but they show that nominal head plus clause is a prototype rather than a rule.

*Restrictive* is the traditional label, and it is close to *integrated* without being identical. An integrated relative can fail to restrict when the head is already unique or when the clause only adds a comment. Integration is structural; restrictiveness is interpretive, and the two can come apart.

blocks.text: *My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida* says two things at once, and the commas mark the seam. The clause is detached, its antecedent is already identified, and what it contributes is information rather than a restriction. Remove it and the sentence still makes a complete claim.

Detachment widens the range of possible antecedents. A supplementary relative can attach to an adjective phrase, as in *Pat is afraid of snakes, which I’m sure Kim is too*, or to a whole clause, as in *Pat is afraid of snakes, which doesn’t surprise me*. It comments on its anchor instead of narrowing it, which is why such loose attachment is possible.

*Non-restrictive* is the usual contrast term, but it names an interpretation rather than a structure. Supplementary relatives are detached and informationally secondary; they are not always non-restrictive in meaning, and integrated relatives are not always restrictive. The two distinctions overlap without coinciding.

blocks.text: Move a relative away from its head and the listener has to work harder to find the antecedent. That is why an integrated relative normally follows its head nominal immediately: adjacency is one of the cues that identifies what the clause modifies. Postposing for emphasis or ease of processing is possible, but the relation stays with the head nominal rather than wandering to whatever noun happens to precede.

Supplementary relatives have more freedom and less tolerance. *My father, who retired last year, now lives in Florida* interrupts the main clause cleanly. Move the same clause to the end, as in *My father now lives in Florida, who retired last year*, and the result is awkward: the relative is separated from its antecedent and lands where a new predication is expected.

Coordination creates genuine ambiguity. *The students and the teachers who attended the meeting* can mean the teachers who attended, or the students and teachers who both attended; the clause can attach to the second coordinate or to the whole coordination.

blocks.text: *A good place from which to watch the procession* and *a good place to watch the procession from* describe the same spot. In the first, the preposition is fronted with *which*; in the second it is stranded at the end and the relative phrase is missing altogether. Both are infinitival relatives, and both leave something understood.

Infinitival relatives are hollow clauses: a non-subject element is missing and gets its interpretation from the head nominal. In *a place to watch the procession from*, the complement of *from* is understood as the place. The head supplies the content; the clause supplies the frame.

The construction is more restricted than its finite counterparts. It clusters after nouns such as *place*, *time*, *way* and *thing*, and it often carries a purpose-like or availability-like meaning: a place to sit, work to do, a way to escape. The interpretation is predictable enough that the missing element rarely needs to be spelled out.

blocks.text: *What he did was outrageous* contains no separate antecedent for *what*. The word does two jobs at once: it stands for the thing, and it marks the relativised element inside the clause. *Whoever devised this plan* and *whichever car appeals to you* work the same way, each fusing antecedent and clause into a single noun phrase.

*Where* and *when* produce fused relatives of a different category. *Put it back where you found it* and *He calls his parents whenever he is in trouble* function as prepositional phrases, not noun phrases, even though their meaning is relative in the ordinary sense. The category follows the word, not the meaning.

A fused relative can look exactly like an open interrogative, and the difference is not always visible in the string. *What he did was outrageous* asserts something about a deed; *What did he do?* asks for the deed. The fused relative has no separate antecedent and functions as a noun phrase, while the interrogative asks for a value. The surrounding predicate usually decides which reading is available.

blocks.text: *The man who she said had won* puts *who* at the front and its gap inside a clause that is itself inside another clause. The link crosses two boundaries without difficulty, and another layer could be added without breaking it. That is what *unbounded* means: the distance between the fronted phrase and its gap is not fixed by the grammar.

The gap keeps its own function. In *the man who she said had won*, it is the subject of *had won*; in *the report which he claimed she had written*, it is the object of *written*. The relative phrase is interpreted through the gap, not through the matrix verb, which is why *said* and *claimed* contribute nothing to the relativised role.

The same machinery operates outside relatives. *Who did she say had won?* has the same long-distance relation as its relative counterpart, and exclamatives and comparatives use it too. Parasitic gaps and antecedent-contained deletion are further cases where one gap depends on another, or where an elided verb phrase is recovered from material that contains it.

blocks.text: The family of relative constructions is wider than the name *relative clause* suggests. It includes wh, that and bare clauses, fused noun phrases and prepositional phrases, and the relatives that appear in clefts. What unites them is a link between a clause-internal position and an antecedent, whether that antecedent is a separate phrase or folded into the relative word itself.

Relational labels describe where the clause sits and what it does there. Integrated relatives modify a nominal and typically restrict it; supplementary relatives are detached and add information about a wider range of anchors; cleft relatives belong to the cleft construction; fused relatives combine antecedent and clause in a single phrase. Infinitival relatives are hollow clauses whose missing element comes from the head.

The mechanics are consistent across the types. A relative phrase can be simple or complex, with the relative feature percolating upward from the word to the larger phrase; relativisation can target subjects, objects, genitives, adjuncts and deeply embedded positions; and the gap always preserves the grammatical function of the element the antecedent interprets.

blocks.title: A relative-construction checklist
blocks.text: Find the antecedent and the relative phrase. Identify the gap and its function. Decide whether the relative is integrated or supplementary, and whether it is wh, that or bare. Then check for fused, cleft or infinitival structure.

options.feedback: The gap preserves the function of the relativised element.

options.text: It is always filled by that.
options.feedback: That is a subordinator, not the gap.

options.text: It only occurs in subject position.
options.feedback: Gaps can be objects, complements, adjuncts and embedded elements.

worked: Take *The report that the committee finally published confirmed what everyone had suspected*. The subject NP is *The report that the committee finally published*. Its head is *report* and the that relative clause modifies it; the gap is the object of published, co-indexed with report.

The object of confirmed is the fused relative NP *what everyone had suspected*. What combines the antecedent and relative word, and the gap after suspected is its object. The example shows an integrated relative inside the subject and a fused relative inside the object, both relying on a gap for interpretation.
application: Start with the antecedent. Identify the relative phrase or gap and the function it has inside the relative clause. Then decide whether the relative is wh, that or bare, and whether it is integrated, supplementary, cleft or fused.

For a complex relative phrase, trace the percolation from the relative word to the larger phrase. In whose house, whose is linked to the antecedent and the whole NP is fronted. In with which, which is linked to the antecedent and the PP is fronted.

For a fused relative, do not look for a separate antecedent. The phrase itself functions as an NP or PP, and the relative word combines the antecedent and the relativised function. Check whether the form is a fused relative or an open interrogative from the syntax and the surrounding predicate.
reveal: In *The report that the committee finally published confirmed what everyone had suspected*, the that clause is an integrated relative modifying report; its gap is the object of published. The fused relative what everyone had suspected is the object of confirmed, and its gap is the object of suspected.
recap: Relative constructions include wh, that and bare clauses, plus fused NP and PP relatives. Integrated relatives modify nominals; supplementary relatives are detached; cleft relatives occur in clefts; fused relatives combine antecedent and relative.

Relativisation involves a gap or relative word linked to an antecedent. Complex relative phrases arise by upward percolation, and the dependency can be unbounded. Infinitival relatives are hollow clauses, and fused relatives must be distinguished from open interrogatives.

self_check.question: What is the difference between a relative clause and a fused relative?
self_check.answer: A relative clause is a clause that modifies an antecedent; a fused relative is a phrase in which antecedent and relative clause are combined, functioning as an NP or PP.

self_check.question: What is upward percolation?
self_check.answer: The spread of a relative feature from a relative word to the larger phrase containing it, as in whose house or with which.

self_check.question: What is an unbounded dependency?
self_check.answer: A relation in which a gap can be embedded arbitrarily deeply while remaining linked to the fronted relative phrase.
